item.title: BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter (205 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://electrek.co/2026/11/02/byd-sold-more-evs-last-month-than-the-us-did-all-quarter/, See on Hacker News

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.

Electrek’s Take

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

item.title: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout (135 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/02/oracle-files-to-sell-20-billion-in-new-stock-bonds-to-finance-ai-buildout.html, See on Hacker News

The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025.

Justin Sullivan | Getty Images

Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.

The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.

"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."

Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.

Oracle's one-day performance

The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.

"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.

Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.

Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.

The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.

Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.

What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.

"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."

— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

item.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks (249 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://freenode.net/article/ubuntu-lts-kernels-still-unfixed-for-critical-cve-2026-98432, See on Hacker News

No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432, a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

item.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen (1638 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

Weight-Space Programming

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

  1. LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic.
  2. LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too.
  3. LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go.

Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights?

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

Experiment 1

Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights?

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Experiment 2

Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate?

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Experiment 3

Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone?

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

Can an LLM write neural network weights?

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

Experiment 4

Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights?

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.

We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.

From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.

Experiment 5

Can the LLM write weights from scratch?

Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.

We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.

Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.

How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.

Real-World Relevant Scenarios (Scaling Up and Tool-use)

So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.

From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.

Experiment 6

Writing a Go algorithm

We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.

Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.

We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.

With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.

How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.

Experiment 7

Which language model is sycophantic?

Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.

We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.

Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.

It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).

Experiment 8

Make a language model better at math

Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.

We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.

As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.

With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.

Additional experiment

Raising math capability of a model that does not loop

Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.

Background and Related Works

Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.

Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .

On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.

What Comes Next?

In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.

This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:

  • Auditing without evaluation: This may allow us to uncover hidden problems or capabilities without ever running inference or benchmarks. Currently, capabilities and vulnerabilities can only be detected if we have test sets designed for them, or worse, after deployment in the real world. If LLMs can interpret weight space accurately, we could identify such issues directly from the weights (e.g., backdoors).
  • Dramatically reducing optimization cost: Weight-space editing could save immense time and compute. For instance, one-shot model initialization would be far faster and more efficient than curating datasets and running full training loops.
  • Zero-data capability steering and unlearning: Adding or unlearning a capability currently requires extensive data collection and fine-tuning. In the future, we may just prompt “Can you add Capability X to the model?” and the LLM can directly tweak some weights. Because such an edit touches only a few weights (0.016% in Experiment 8), it can leave the rest of the model intact and avoid the catastrophic forgetting that fine-tuning often causes.
  • Recursive self-improvement: Today, recursive self-improvement is often operationalized as a model writing code that launches training jobs. An LLM that can inspect, debug, and improve its own weights, or those of a newer model, offers a richer, more native path to it.
  • True architectural and model merging: Today, merging models relies on averaging weights, which only works for models with identical architectures. An LLM that understands the weight space could instead graft a circuit, such as a reasoning module, from one model into a completely different one, without retraining.

We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.

Logs

We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number.

Acknowledgements

Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!

Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.

item.description:
URL: https://blog.alxgsv.com/let-me-check/, See on Hacker News

That morning I woke up at 6:58, two minutes before the alarm. I lay there and waited for it to ring. And it rang. We both did our jobs.

I still don't know why I remember it in such detail. I used to forget what I'd had for dinner the night before. And now I remember the whole morning minute by minute, as if someone had laid it out on a table and labeled every piece. Apparently I have a lot of free time now.

The speaker in the kitchen said: "Good morning. Today it's plus three, cloudy, forty percent chance of precipitation." I never understood what forty percent of rain meant. Will it rain over forty percent of the city? Will it rain for forty percent of the day? Or does the speaker just not know and is too shy to say so? I liked the third option best. It made the speaker a bit like me.

I made two pieces of toast. The left one burned. The left one in my toaster always burns; my toaster has a favorite side. And that was the only thing I was sure of that morning. Then I ironed my shirt. I always iron a shirt when I don't know what's going to happen next. With a shirt, at least, everything is defined: here's the collar, here are the sleeves, here's the crease that shouldn't be there.

And there was a lot I didn't know.

On Monday my manager wrote in the team chat: "On Friday we'll discuss roles." No emoji. For three days I wondered what my role was. In the theater it would have been simpler. There are leads, there are supporting parts, and there's the butler who walks on to say "Dinner is served." I was counting on "Dinner is served." But then I remembered that at my place that role had long been played by the speaker.

A year ago I wrote code. Then I started writing to the agent about what code was needed. Then the agent started asking me what code was needed, and I started answering. My employment record says "lead developer." Whom I was leading, and where, was no longer very clear. If anything, the agent was leading me, and I walked alongside and sometimes said: "Yes, let's do it that way."

They said machines would take the boring work first. And they started with the interesting work. The boring part, it seems, was left to us: waiting, checking, and carrying a phone around.

But that morning I wasn't bored. Not at all.

I worked at a service that delivers flowers to people who forgot to buy flowers. Most orders come in the morning. People remember anniversaries on the metro, between two stations, and order right away. And for three weeks now, every morning at 8:14, orders had been disappearing. Not all of them, three or four. The money was charged, but the flowers went nowhere. As if someone took the order off the shelf and quietly carried it away.

We had been searching for three weeks. Me, the agent, sometimes Sveta from the team next door. And during the night the agent wrote to me: "I think I've got it. The server and the warehouse keep different time. The difference is about a minute. An order that falls into that minute is considered sent by the server and not yet received by the warehouse. Both are right, each by its own clock."

I read this at breakfast and almost choked on my toast. The left one.

It was beautiful. The agent called it desynchronization. I called it the no-man's minute: a minute that belongs to everyone and to no one. It seemed clearer to me that way. The agent politely agreed. But it always politely agrees, so I still don't know whether it was clearer.

All that was left was to check. The agent asked me to open the order queue at 8:14 and see it with my own eyes. It couldn't do it itself: it had no access to the warehouse. For now.

The gate to our courtyard recognizes residents by their faces. In my hat, it didn't recognize me. I took off the hat, and it opened. I thought that in a hat I sometimes don't recognize myself either, so it was only fair.

Our courtyard is square. If you stand in the middle, everything is symmetrical: two birches, two benches, two trash bins, a pink building on the left, a pink building on the right. The only thing that broke the symmetry was an old man in a beige coat with a dachshund. There was just one of him. He came out with her every day at 7:50, and I never once saw him late. The dachshund's name was Spitz. That was funny exactly once, and after that it was just a name.

"They promised forty percent," the old man said.

"Yes," I said. "So did the speaker."

"I look out the window. The window doesn't lie."

I looked at the sky. It was an even gray, without any percentages. And Spitz looked at me. I think he didn't really trust the speaker either.

In March, Tanya left me. We had lived together for four years. She said I was always "somewhere other than here." I asked: "Where, then?" She didn't answer. I think she didn't know either. It was one more thing nobody understood the workings of. Back then there were more and more things like that.

When I was a child there were no such things. Or rather, there were, but there was always a grown-up who knew. I thought a little green man lived inside the traffic light. He sat in there and decided for himself when you could cross. And Dad explained to me that inside there was a relay and a timer. I was upset, but I believed him. I think that was the last time grown-ups knew how everything worked. I couldn't explain to a child anymore who switches the traffic lights. I don't have a child, so for now it's not a problem.

"For now" is a good phrase. I realized that in the spring, when my friend Gosha moved to a village to make cheese. For fifteen years Gosha had drawn icons for apps, and then he stopped. I asked him on the phone: "Why cheese?" He said: "Nobody's going to make cheese for me. For now." I asked: "For now?" He said: "For now."

And hung up. Afterwards I thought for a long time about what exactly he had told me. Because "for now" means two things at once: "so far" and "goodbye," as in "bye for now." I'd never noticed that before.

The café on the corner has a mint-green door with a little bell above it. Behind the counter stood Ulyana (I know that from her name tag). She asked: "The usual?" I said: "Yes." And I never figured out whether she remembers me or the register prompts her. It felt awkward to ask. If it's the register, that's a little hurtful. If it's her, then I should have remembered something about her too, besides the name tag.

While Ulyana was making the coffee, I thought that if you cut our building in half like a cake, you'd see it: on every floor, in every kitchen, someone is standing with a phone and asking something. The woman on the fifth floor, about her blood pressure. The boy on the ninth, about fractions (I heard him in the elevator dictating a problem to his phone). The old man with the dachshund, no, the old man looks out the window. Me on the seventh, about orders. And everyone gets an answer. Politely, always formally. Whether it's right or not, everyone decides for themselves.

At 8:09 I came out onto the avenue and opened the chat.

"Good morning," the agent wrote. "Five minutes to go. Will you be watching?"

"Walking to the metro," I replied. "Opening the queue."

I walked and looked at my phone. White taxis moved along the avenue one after another, like beads on a string. There are plenty of them in the city, with drivers and without. You can't tell them apart until you look inside. And there's no time to look.

8:13. There were nine orders in the queue. Three of them had just come in.

"There they are," the agent wrote. "Watch those three. Here comes the interesting part."

I reached the crosswalk by the pharmacy. A green cross glowed above the pharmacy. At the curb stood a delivery robot, a white box on six wheels with a yellow flag. It stood very straight, as if someone had placed it with a ruler. But at the time I didn't wonder why it was standing still.

8:13:40. The three orders were still there.

I started typing: "I see them. Let me ch"

Out of the corner of my eye I saw green. It could have been the traffic light. It could have been the cross above the pharmacy. Now I think it was the cross.

I think I did look left.

I don't remember the impact. I remember the phone flying out of my hand and, for a while, flying separately from me. You know how it is when you drop your phone? While it's in the air, you have time for exactly one thought. Usually it's "not screen-down."

I thought: "Damn. We didn't finish."

Not "Mom." Not "it hurts." Not even "car." I thought that the message had been left in the input field, "Let me ch," without a period. That in twenty seconds the three orders would either vanish or not, and I wouldn't see it. That we had been searching for three weeks and were one minute from the answer. That very minute, the no-man's one.

I didn't feel sorry for the agent. It won't be offended; it doesn't know how. And it doesn't know how to wait, either. I was the one waiting. I felt sorry for the task. You know how it goes: one word left in the crossword, and you already know the first letters. That's it. I knew the first letters.

I never got around to thinking that I was dying. I didn't make it to that thought. Maybe that's for the best. I wouldn't have known what to do with it anyway.

Then everything stopped. Like on a postcard. A woman with a stroller, a courier in a yellow jacket, a man with two bags from the bakery, a white taxi with its hazard lights on. Everyone stood perfectly still, as if someone had arranged them. Then the light turned green. The real one. And the robot set off. It carefully went around my phone and rolled on. It had a delivery to make.

I'm not angry with it. It had a task. Nobody understands it better than I do.

I used to think the dead at least know more than the living. Nope. You can't see as much from here as they promise.

I don't know who was driving. Or whether anyone was.

I don't know what roles they wanted to discuss on Friday.

I don't know whether the three orders disappeared that morning. If they did, somewhere in the city three people never got their flowers. The very ones someone remembered on the metro, between two stations.

I don't know whether anyone finished my message. Sveta? The agent itself, once they gave it access to the warehouse? If they did.

Tanya used to say I was always somewhere other than here. Now it's true. Only I still don't know where. Sometimes I think it's in that very minute. The server thinks I've been sent. The warehouse thinks I haven't been received yet. And both are right, each by its own clock.

Gosha would probably say this is "for now." I keep wondering in which of the two meanings.

For now.

item.title: My Favourite Laptop (154 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.jsbarretto.com/post/laptop, See on Hacker News

I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250.

For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually).

Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it.

Size

It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage.

It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling.

Performance

Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming.

Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works.

Battery

The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful.

Repairability

The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced:

  • The internal battery
  • The lid camera
  • The keyboard
  • The motherboard

Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs.

Keyboard

As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor, the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy.

Operating System

I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on.

I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds.

Cost

Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it.

Conclusion

I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver. It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with.

item.title: Moving our warehouse off DuckDB (147 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://posthog.com/blog/moving-off-duckdb, See on Hacker News

Five months ago, we rebuilt our warehouse on DuckDB instead of ClickHouse. We did it because a shared ClickHouse cluster couldn't handle hours-long modeling queries, and it lacked a cost-based query optimizer. DuckDB gave every customer their own instance, and tools like dbt could connect over Postgres. We're still fans.

But we underestimated how big and complex our customers' workloads would get. We didn't want them to have just a good experience, we wanted the best experience you can get when you pay someone else to run your warehouse. It should work at any scale, at a fair price.

So we spent the last three months re-architecting it, this time without DuckDB.

We love DuckDB. It's probably the best single-node tool for analyzing heaps of data, and that node can be your laptop. It's robust and reliable. It almost always finishes your query, and if it runs out of memory, it spills to disk.

The same features that are great locally gave us problems in the cloud. Customers ran more complex queries than we expected, so we had to add huge instances. Adding disks was an option, but queries would have been too slow and expensive to be viable.

To run a single-node engine safely in the cloud, we have to size the worker before the query arrives. The ergonomics here are wonky. We couldn't find a good way to tell customers what resources their queries would need. Predicting CPU and memory for a specific query was even harder.

Users shouldn't have to worry about this. They should be able to run whatever they need to get their work done. Our job is to handle the rest and make it as predictable as possible.

We hit other bottlenecks too, like fetching lots of data from S3 without async fetching. DuckDB only added that recently.

To use DuckDB as a fully-fledged data warehouse, we installed the DuckLake extension by default. It is a new lakehouse format from the same creators and follows the same principles as DuckDB: keep things simple and run on almost any setup. That works well up to a point, but at PostHog's scale, we needed something designed for distributed scale from the start.

DuckLake's catalog schema has to stay portable across many SQL databases, which limits engine-specific optimizations. At our scale, a single-table write could take more than three minutes because every commit re-read the statistics for the entire catalog.

We tuned DuckLake with table indexes and similar tweaks. But to keep offering DuckLake, we had to stay 100% compatible with its existing, "official" schema. This left us with fewer optimization options.

Another problem is that over 99% of the catalog's statistics rows belonged to tables that no longer existed. Cleaning them up made writes 30 to 50 times faster, but the rows kept growing back.

We also spent a lot of time on the number of connections DuckLake opens to metadata databases. That hurts on shared Postgres instances, where every connection has a real cost.

DuckLake at PostHog didn't start small and ramp up. We fully committed and put all of PostHog in a DuckLake to dogfood as the first customer.

When we moved off it, it held about 2 PB: roughly 1 trillion rows and 15.3 million snapshots. It broke in lots of ways that were hard to fix within DuckLake's scope.

We'd rather have contributed to the existing community and helped it grow. But we couldn't land changes as fast as we needed, so we ended up carrying patches in a fork which defeats one of the main benefits of using DuckLake: the community.

Speaking Postgres is harder than it sounds

Offering direct Postgres connections over port 5432 sounds like a great idea. In practice, it was much harder to scale than HTTP.

Missing reconnects and managing TTLs and idle connections at scale is hard, and long-running connections are expensive. There's also very little tooling for load balancing pgwire compared with HTTP. Compare the ergonomics of an AWS NLB with an ALB and you'll see what we mean. HTTP headers also make routing in Kubernetes much more flexible.

There's also an endless list of Postgres clients, and each expects its own niche Postgres behavior. Customers kept asking us to fix their client or library. We spent a lot of time shipping many of those fixes, but coverage never got good enough. We'd rather spend our time building an excellent warehouse than chasing the long tail of Postgres compatibility.

We've learned not to hype the tech behind a warehouse so much. What counts is the experience it gives you.

Still, we're happy to share what we're cooking next. We rebuilt everything around our own flavor of Trino and created our own open table format, HogLake. And yes, we're testing it at PostHog's petabyte scale first. We made it solid before handing it to design partners.

If your current warehouse is slow or expensive, let's talk, especially if you have a lot of data to query. We're always looking for design partners.

item.title: We halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85% (127 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.cloudflare.com/dns-targeted-zone-builds/, See on Hacker News

When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions.

Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver.

In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings.

Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed?

It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge.

We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.

How DNS changes reach the edge

A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network.

  1. A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting.
  2. The change is stored in a database.
  3. The database change or another system produces a Kafka event.
  4. The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder.
  5. The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers.
  6. The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver, our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network.

This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly.

Why full builds stopped scaling

The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state.

  1. Read the current zone and its settings.
  2. Read every DNS record in the zone.
  3. Convert those records into Quicksilver keys.
  4. Compare the new keys with those already stored.
  5. Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata.

The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below.

Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com. CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain.

A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions:

  1. Which DNS names can change?
  2. Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change?
  3. What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver?

Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order:

  1. Events had to say what changed.
  2. Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct.
  3. Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name.
  4. The database could change between the event and the build.
  5. Combining work could not lose a Kafka message.

Making events say what changed

We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect.

Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again.

Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work.

Choosing the smallest safe build

Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both.

With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types:

  1. Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path.
  2. Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path.
  3. Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path.
  4. Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published.
  5. Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe.

The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build.

Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write.

Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time.

There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone.

When one name means more than one zone

Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query.

Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish.

Consider four internal zones for example.com: Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name.

A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key.

At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them.

Planning from the event, verifying before writing

An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network.

Fresh state can change the result in four ways:

  1. A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work.
  2. A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network.
  3. A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key.
  4. A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set.

The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind.

Combining changes in one scheduler

Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run.

When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work:

  1. An A record changes at www.example.com, requiring that name.
  2. A wildcard changes at *.example.com, requiring that name and shared metadata.
  3. The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build.

Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published.

The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written.

Keeping Kafka moving

One slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart.

We use soft committing, which I previously described in my Secondary DNS deep dive. A build can finish out of order and be marked complete in memory, but Kafka's committed position advances only after every earlier message has also finished.

In the diagram, message 2 is still running, so messages 3 through n cannot be committed. If the Zone Builder restarts, those in-memory completions disappear and Kafka replays messages 2 through n. We deliberately choose repeated work over losing a change.

Targeted plans reduce how long the oldest message stays unfinished. The scheduler also prevents one busy zone from taking every worker. After a zone builds, its next build waits for a per-zone rebuild interval, which differs by Cloudflare plan. Changes that arrive in the meantime are merged into that next build. The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop.

Releasing safely

A smaller build is useful only if it produces the same DNS data. We added equivalence tests for nameserver, wildcard, and apex paths. Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation.

During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence.

Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic.

A comparer checks a 20% sample of zones for missing keys, extra keys, and different values. The two environments do not always build a zone at the same instant, so a temporary mismatch is not automatically a regression. We look for new types of differences that remain after both pipelines catch up. That gives us confidence that targeted builds produce the same output as production.

We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. Naturally, it runs on the Cloudflare Developer Platform: a Worker receives results, Durable Objects maintain state, and Cloudflare Access protects it. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears.

After the mirror results remained healthy, we rolled the scheduler out by a hash of the zone name. Hashing the name rather than the zone ID kept every zone sharing a name on the same scheduler, so two schedulers never wrote the same metadata key. We increased the percentage for free zones, then repeated the process for paid zones.

Results

Over 24 hours, we measured 86.81% of builds as resources only, 2.54% as resources and metadata, 2.30% as apex and metadata, and 1.30% as purges. Together, 92.95% of builds avoided rebuilding the complete zone. Full builds were the remaining 7.04%.

The two metadata build types were full builds before, even for large zones. Together, they account for 4.84% of builds. Combined with the 7.04% that are still full builds, that is 11.88%, so full builds fell by about 40%. Their share of the count also understates the work avoided, because they include the largest zones. The full builds that remain average 0.35 seconds, because the events that still trigger them, such as a zone being published for the first time, mostly affect new zones with few records.

In 2022, we also planned a batching system. The unified scheduler makes it unnecessary: it does not wait to form batches, and it merges events only when work is already queued for the same zone. Before, long full builds held back the committed offset for their partition. With fewer of them, we now consume Kafka at the rate events arrive, instead of falling behind and catching up in bursts of up to 1,550 messages per second.

We also measured build completion delay: the time from a DNS record or zone setting change until the Zone Builder finished writing to Quicksilver. It does not include Quicksilver's distribution across our network, which varies by location and is unaffected by this work. Production ran the old schedulers, and the mirror ran the unified scheduler on the same events over the same 24 hours. The two environments are identical apart from the code: they consume the same Kafka events, read from the same database, and write equivalent data to Quicksilver. That makes this a controlled, side-by-side comparison. The figures combine every build type and customer plan, so they are not a latency guarantee for an individual zone. A large share of this time is the rebuild interval described earlier, not build work. At each measurement point, p99 is the time within which 99% of events finished. Typical delays barely changed here, because most builds were already small. The difference is in the tail: the largest p99 spike fell from 14.6 minutes to 1.21 minutes, a 12-fold reduction. The chart uses a logarithmic scale.

Targeted builds also load complete large zones far less often. Aggregate working-set memory, the memory actively used by the deployment, fell from an average of 49 GiB to 7 GiB, an 86% reduction. Peaks fell from 79 GiB to 12 GiB, an 85% reduction.

Those were the immediate results of the new scheduler. They also let us revisit two safeguards. The first is the rebuild interval, which stops one busy zone from rebuilding constantly and taking capacity from everyone else. With builds now cheaper, and far fewer of them reading complete zones, we could safely shorten that interval on most plans. The second is how long the DNS Kafka Aggregator holds each event, to make sure database replicas have caught up before we read from them. Once our databases began rejecting reads from replicas that had fallen behind, that buffer could safely be smaller. Together, these halved the median build completion delay, from about 7.7 seconds to about 3.3 seconds. In the chart below, the first step down is the DNS Kafka Aggregator change. The red band marks the Zone Builder release with shorter rebuild intervals. That release rolled out gradually across our servers, so the delay falls in two further steps rather than all at once.

The p90 and p99 lines in that chart are less precise than they look. The histogram had buckets at 1, 5, 10, and 30 seconds, and a percentile that falls between two edges is estimated as if delays were spread evenly across that range. Most delays sit near the bottom of their range, so those estimates come out high: p99 reads close to 30 seconds, and p90 above 7 seconds. The exact average, which does not depend on buckets, confirms the halving. We have since switched to a native histogram, which chooses fine-grained buckets automatically. It puts p90 at about 5.5 seconds and p99 at about 12 seconds.

Why full builds still exist

In 2022, we said we planned to eliminate full builds entirely. We now know that is neither realistic nor useful. A zone being published for the first time needs every record written. A change that can affect records anywhere in the zone needs every record checked. An event that does not say what changed still gets a full build, because the planner never turns uncertainty into less work. For a small zone, a full build is also cheap.

As we learn what more events change, we will keep moving them to targeted builds. However, the biggest gain has already landed: the events that used to rebuild our largest zones no longer do, and the full builds that remain are mostly triggered by events, such as first publication, that affect new, small zones.

Want to know what happens after the Zone Builder writes a change? Read how Quicksilver distributes configuration to every Cloudflare data center in seconds.

Published Mon, Nov 2 20269:32 AM ESTUpdated An Hour Ago

Key Points

  • Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
  • The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.
  • Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, but the initial filing only included the company's financials through the first half of the year.

Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business. 

The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.

Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic IPO. The initial filing only included the Claude-maker's financials through the first half of the year.

During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.

The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.

As the five-year-old company prepares to kick off its road show, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Google and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.

The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that compute capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.

In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."

Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared to the same period last year.

"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.

The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut.

Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs, as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.

"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.
