item.title: Sam Altman: All the RAM Should Belong to Me, So I Can Charge People to Use It (118 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://gizmodo.com/sam-altman-all-the-ram-should-belong-to-me-so-i-can-charge-people-to-use-it-2000833412, See on Hacker News

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is really gunning for villain-of-the-year status with PC gamers in particular, but owners of pretty much any computing device everywhere.

Altman appeared on Stripe cofounder John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast this week, sipping beers and weighing in on the state of AI. Gizmodo covered and analyzed the bulk of Altman’s remarks here, though another moment from the podcast is worthy of a shout-out. Altman thinks it’s “quite terrible” that individual device owners and/or operators of local AIs have access to DRAM, which is already catastrophically expensive due to massive demand from AI data centers like OpenAI’s (and may be nowhere close to peaking).

You see, it’s inefficient not to just let OpenAI handle it. “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center,” Altman said.

“But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time,” he added. “You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

There is an unobjectionable point buried somewhere in there. Perhaps a future utopian society could provide universal access to centralized compute. But there’s a more obnoxious point that doesn’t need excavating: Altman isn’t describing the optimal distribution of resources so much as the distribution of resources optimal to him. That arrangement would entail DRAM manufacturers devote even more capacity to fueling OpenAI’s incomprehensibly expensive infrastructure rollout ($750 billion through 2030!) and consumers delegate ever-increasing control of their work and lives to AI assistants. The cost of that rollout is directly driving up prices of DRAM and other components through the roof, even for products like smartphones. Closed-source data centers are OpenAI’s bread and butter, as is platformization and consolidation.

Presumably the dream is that any time someone needs to write a document, call someone, stream media, play a video game, or do pretty much anything else that requires computation, they pay an OpenAI cloud agent based in a data center to do it. But hey, they won’t need to worry about paying for RAM, right?

Anyhow, Altman can pry my RAM from my cold, dead fingers—and he’ll probably have to, because it doesn’t look like 32GB DDR5 will drop below $450 or more anytime soon, or ever.

item.title: If you love a website, back it up (343 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.mistys-internet.website/post/2026/10/29/if-you-love-a-website-back-it-up/, See on Hacker News

This story starts with a little tragedy. See, I’ve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. There’s websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and there’s something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes.

There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken. It’s about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea.1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads.

I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didn’t. This post is here to beg you to do what I didn’t think to, and to teach you how.

You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe it’s something they couldn’t do. It’s something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But that’s not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can, but should! Don’t just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you don’t want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up!

All of the tools I’ll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC2. You don’t have to worry about any of the technical details3, but I’m telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post:

You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. It’s an entire website right in a post! (And if you don’t trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose “download archive”, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!)

By the way, for disclosure: the tools I’m going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but that’s not because they’ll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving.

Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension

By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesn’t take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is:

  1. Install the browser extension.
  2. Visit the first page you want to archive.
  3. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Start Archiving”.
  4. If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads.
  5. Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them.
  6. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Stop Archiving”.

You’re done! You just archived a web page! Now that it’s all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extension’s icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you archived, load them in browser, and see if they work. (I’ll go into more details on how you can look at web archives and share them with others later in this post.)

Option 2 - archiveweb.page app

If you don’t want to install a browser extension, or you don’t have Chrome installed, you can also grab the standalone archiveweb.page app. This is basically the same thing as the browser extension above, it just has its own web browser built in. It also opens straight to the menu that lets you browse your web archives, so it’s a handy way to look at your web archives locally. Pretty much everything else I described above applies.

Option 3 - Browsertrix

The above options are great for single pages or sites that are small enough for you to browse manually. But if you’ve got a webpage that’s big enough that it’s going to be annoying visiting all of the pages by hand, you probably want to look at a web crawler tool for web archiving. There are a bunch of options out there, but the easiest to use as an individual is probably Browsertrix. A web crawler is basically an automation tool built around a web browser; you provide instructions on what page to start from and what pages it should visit, and it will go ahead and click links to automatically find pages so that it can archive the page as completely as possible. The web archive I embedded above was done using Browsertrix on pretty close to its default settings: I just told it I wanted to do a site crawl for the entire domain https://teapuppies.mistys-internet.website, and it worked it out from there:

But, depending, on what you’re looking for, it has options which can be customized to narrow down what content it archives. For example, if you decided you only want pages for the episodes, you could tell it to only capture anything at the /episodes/ section of the website:

Or even just a single page and anything that page links to:

There are a lot more options than I can go into in a quick overview - it’s a comprehensive tool with a lot of options. But if you’re looking to archive a whole website, or a complete social media profile, I’d recommend giving it a try.

Unlike the other tools, which you mainly run on your own computer, Browsertrix is primarily a web app. It’s also the only paid tool in this post - there’s a seven day trial, but after that you do have to pay per use. Since it’s open source, though, technically inclined users can run their own copies on their computer or deploy a copy somewhere if they like.

Viewing your archived webpage

Once you’ve actually backed the site up, you can replay it to use it in your browser just like a live webpage. It’s kind of like having your own private version of the wayback machine. You can test it out yourself for your own private use using the interface built into the version of archiveweb.page you used, but if you want to share it with someone else you have a few options. If you want to share it with someone privately, you can send them the WARC/WACZ file and let them load it into the ArchiveWeb.page app or the ReplayWeb.page website. If you want to share it with the world, though, you can set up a website with your web archive on it.

This post is using the ReplayWeb.page embedded viewer, which is open source and can be embedded inside any other web page you want. You don’t have run any kind of app on your server to do this; as long as you have the ability to upload the archive and a little bit of JavaScript, you can easily add a copy of the replay interface into any web page or blog post.

Preserving the data once you have it

Since everything you backed up is bundled inside a single WACZ file, it’s really easy to keep safe - or share with someone else. Lots of copies keeps stuff safe, after all; if you think you have friends who’d like to hold on to a copy of whatever site you’ve backed it up, pass it along and share the duty of preserving it!

If any of this sounds interesting to you, I’d encourage you to at least give it a try. I’d love for the world to be filled with thousands upon thousands of little web archives, with people and community groups archiving and sharing the things that matter to them for themselves. If you’re finding any of this overwhelming, and you’re not sure where to get started, please reach out to me - I’m very happy to give you a hand.

Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”

French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.

Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.

Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.

Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.

They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.

ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

item.title: Supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden hit by suspected cyber-attack (108 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cq1kd1nee80eo, See on Hacker News

Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".

He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.

Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.

"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.

The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.

In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.

Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.

In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.

The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.

Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.

Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".

In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.

A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".

"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.

One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."

The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.

Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.

The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.

The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.

In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.

A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.

A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

API

curl https://api.syscall.sh/v2/syscalls/x64/read

Any kernel release, diffs between releases and more in the API docs.

Syscall tables across kernel versions

Entries get added and, rarely, removed between releases. Each architecture page has a kernel selector, and its JSON download records when each entry first appeared (since) and when it was dropped (removed_in).

Removed entries stay visible: pick "all, with removed" in the kernel selector and each dropped syscall is marked with the release that dropped it.

Where the data comes from

Everything on this site is read from the kernel source itself. For each architecture, the generator walks the syscall table and the SYSCALL_DEFINE macros of every mainline release it scans, so these are the numbers the kernel actually dispatches on.

It also records each architecture's calling convention, the instruction that enters the kernel, so every syscall table shows exactly where the number and the arguments go.

A syscall whose since equals the first release scanned for its architecture was already there back then, and may be much older.

Descriptions and full history

The short descriptions come from the Linux man pages project, and the io_uring ones from liburing. Whenever the data changes, the site is rebuilt from the syscall API.

item.title: BioWare co-founder: game execs "have never made a game" and don't get it (120 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.pcgamer.com/gaming-industry/none-of-these-people-have-ever-made-a-game-bioware-co-founder-greg-zeschuk-says-of-game-industry-executives-they-just-dont-know-how-it-works/, See on Hacker News

It's been almost 15 years since BioWare co-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka announced their retirements from the videogame industry, and they've been resolute about staying out of it ever since: Muzyka continues to head up the ThresholdImpact investment firm he founded in 2012 and holds multiple roles at the University of Alberta, while Zeschuk owns Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company, also based in Alberta, where he works with a small handful of other BioWare veterans.

But Zeschuk stepped back into the videogame spotlight, briefly, following last week's closure of BioWare by parent company Electronic Arts, telling 80lv that he got the news hours after it happened because he was on a fishing trip, and by the time he flew home a couple days later, he'd "already shelved it away."

"I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it," Zeschuk said. "I’m not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck. And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that."

Zeschuk said he had his own "emotional moment" about BioWare years ago, when he left the company; his real concern now is for the people at the studio who now find themselves out of work: "Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad."

He also said he has no regrets about the EA acquisition, saying it offered "stability" as the studio continued to grow and that "we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks." At the same time, he had a feeling when EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's PIF that it probably wouldn't go well for BioWare, because it doesn't fit into the guns-and-sports model: "BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways."

Zeschuk was also critical of the idea, seen in the recent wave of studio mergers and AI-powered cutbacks, "that you can just kind of recreate great games with random people and AI. It doesn't work," Zeschuk said.

"The other harsh reality of almost all these companies, the people that go down the business track never really come from the development track. Because none of these people have ever made a game, like, never really sat and made one, like, from start to finish, even a small thing, they just don't know how it works."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Zeschuk does know how it works, and he was clear that he's not interested in going back. "For me it was time to go, and I kind of walked out of the games business without any intention of ever returning. I'm happy being a consumer and playing games," he said. "I have my opinions on how to make stuff, but as enticing as it would be, it's just not [worth] the personal struggle and cost and effort required to make a great game. Having gone through the crucible of game development, I'm not going back in there."

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

item.title: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48 (146 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-china-ai-export-controls-announcement-48-2/, See on Hacker News

Key Takeaways

On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1].

The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1].

The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4].

Background

China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6].

Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. The official annex groups the AI items into large models, agents, compute clusters, chip design, and information-processing technologies. It also excludes from management any technology that has already entered the public domain through open-source release or academic publication [1].

The interim registration requirement is the part that applies today. From the announcement date until the revised catalogue takes effect, exporters must register through MOFCOM’s unified business platform before exporting any listed technology. Registration covers four triggers: transfer of technology ownership abroad, licensing of domestic technology for overseas use, a change in ownership or control that makes a foreign entity the owner or controller, and other cases MOFCOM designates [2][4]. Exporters must decide for themselves whether a technology falls within scope. The registration form asks for recipient details, destination, technology description, end use, and estimated value [2][4].

The timing also matters for enterprises that already track U.S. controls. CSA’s prior research documented the first U.S. use of export-control authority to suspend a broadly deployed commercial frontier model [9]. Announcement No. 48 means frontier AI supply chains now face formal outbound controls from both of the largest AI-producing jurisdictions. ChinaTalk observes that the 10^26 FLOP threshold mirrors the figure used in the 2023 U.S. executive order and the since-rescinded 2025 U.S. AI Diffusion rule. The authors also estimate that no released Chinese model currently exceeds it [3].

Security Analysis

What the AI Annex Actually Controls

The annex is granular, and its structure matters for scoping. The table below summarizes the AI items drawn from the official draft annex [1], with interpretive notes from published analyses [3][4].

Category Control Key Thresholds or Conditions (draft)
Large models trained on China’s “core data” Prohibited Core data scope defined by the Data Security Law and related regulations
Large models trained on China’s “important data” Restricted Excludes trace use (≤0.1%) of desensitized important data that does not materially improve capability or reappear in outputs, and lawfully public data
Core large-model technologies (weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, training and inference optimization) Restricted Any one of: ≥10^26 FLOPs; ≥2 trillion parameters; global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export
High-performance agents for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government Prohibited Agent meets the restricted agent thresholds and is specially or mainly designed for those uses
Agent planning and task decomposition Restricted ≥20-step subtask chains, ≥80% decomposition accuracy, ≥90% subtask success
Multi-agent collaboration architectures Restricted ≥60 concurrent agents, completion time ≤2x the single-agent minimum, ≥85% agreement with reference answers
Tool calling and system operation Restricted ≥200 integrated third-party tools, ≥90% tool-selection accuracy, ≥90% end-to-end success on tasks requiring 3+ tools
AI malicious code generation, adaptive evasion, and variant generation Prohibited Attack-success and automation thresholds, where usable against high-sensitivity systems
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery Restricted Any of six tests, including ≥75% on authoritative benchmarks, 10x senior-expert efficiency, or autonomous chaining of 2+ low or medium flaws into a working exploit
AI detection technology specially designed for cross-border data security Prohibited Detection accuracy and recall ≥95%
Deepfake detection; steganography; voiceprint; Chinese and minority-language translation Restricted Accuracy, recall, latency, and fidelity thresholds (for example, ≥98% for deepfake detection)
AI chip and memory chip design; large compute cluster technologies Restricted Process node ≤14 nm and other alternative criteria for AI chips; interconnect ≥800 GB/s, fault tolerance, and heterogeneous scheduling for clusters above 10,000 accelerators

Three features of this structure deserve attention from security and compliance teams. First, the “global leading” test is dynamic. A model that falls below the compute and parameter thresholds can still become restricted if its public evaluation rank, global call volume, or similar measures place it in the top 10 when the export occurs [1]. ChinaTalk calls this criterion “by far the most up-for-interpretation,” noting that the rule names no ranking body [3], and it means the compliance status of a given model version can change after deployment. Second, the agent items are defined by system behavior rather than by the underlying model. An orchestration framework that integrates hundreds of tools could meet the tool-use threshold even when it runs on a model well below the frontier thresholds, an issue Ray Sun identifies as unresolved [5]. Third, the cyber items carry direct security consequences: Chinese-origin AI red-teaming, vulnerability-discovery, and detection tools that meet the thresholds would require a license to leave China, and offensive code-generation capability could not be exported at all.

Deployment Models and Where the Line Falls

MOFCOM’s spokesperson framed the central test as whether restricted technology moves from inside China to overseas [2]. That framing produces a clear distinction between consuming a model as a service and taking custody of it, as summarized below.

Deployment scenario Treatment under MOFCOM guidance
API calls, apps or websites, SaaS for overseas customers Not within large-model export management [2]
Lightweight on-device deployment Not within large-model export management [2]
Local deployment of a restricted model on infrastructure outside China Within export management; license required [2]
Deployment on a Chinese company’s self-operated overseas cloud or compute center Automatic licensing (“report and export”) may apply [2]
Open-sourcing newly developed restricted technology Automatic licensing after reporting [2]
Technology already public via open-source release or academic papers Outside management scope [1]

For enterprises, the practical consequence is that the deployment model the draft captures, local self-hosting, is also the one often chosen for data-protection reasons. Organizations that chose to self-host a Chinese frontier model in their own environment, rather than call a Chinese-hosted API, did so to keep sensitive data inside their own boundary. MOFCOM places local deployment outside China within export management, which means those self-hosting arrangements require the Chinese supplier to hold a license [2]. ChinaTalk reads this as also covering on-premises licensing deals and managed deployments in which a vendor runs an agent’s reasoning loop inside a customer environment [3]. Because licenses can be revoked or conditioned, ChinaTalk suggests this may lead some non-Chinese users to reconsider such dependencies [3]. The registration requirement already covers exports in progress, so ongoing weight-delivery or model-update arrangements may be affected now rather than after the catalogue is finalized [2].

The treatment of open weights depends on whether a model is already public. Weights that are already public are outside the controls [1]. Open-sourcing a new restricted model, however, falls under automatic licensing that still requires reporting [2]. Commentators note that “open source” is not defined, and that it is unclear how restricted-use licenses would be treated [3]. Organizations that depend on successive open-weight releases from Chinese labs should therefore treat future release cadence, not just current availability, as a variable outside their control.

Exposure Through Corporate Structure

The exposure most likely to surprise multinationals sits in their own organizational charts. Registration is triggered by licensing technology for overseas use and by changes of ownership or control, not only by sales to third parties [2][4]. A multinational with China-based R&D teams building agent frameworks, vulnerability-discovery tooling, or fine-tuned models may therefore need to register before sharing that work with affiliates outside China. ChinaTalk reads the registration form’s field on exports made outside formal contracts as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing and open-sourcing [3]. This reading is an inference from the form rather than an official statement, but it is a reasonable basis for conservative scoping.

The data-based items add a second pathway. A model fine-tuned in China on operational data that qualifies as “important data” under the Data Security Law would be restricted, unless the de minimis carve-out applies. A model trained on “core data” would be prohibited [1]. Organizations that classified China-resident data under the Data Security Law for cross-border data transfer purposes may not have applied the same classification to training and fine-tuning datasets, since those obligations previously governed data transfer rather than model transfer.

Finally, recent precedent suggests that redomiciling does not remove Chinese jurisdiction. In January 2026, MOFCOM announced an assessment of Meta’s acquisition of Manus, a Singapore-registered AI agent company whose products were developed in China. The assessment examined whether the relocation of staff and technology required export authorization [7]. Announcement No. 48 now gives that line of scrutiny explicit, agent-specific thresholds, which suggests M&A due diligence on AI targets with China-origin development history should include an export-control workstream.

Recommendations

Immediate Actions

Organizations should first inventory every Chinese-origin model, agent framework, and AI security tool in use and record how each is consumed: as an API or SaaS service, as a lightweight on-device component, or as locally deployed weights or code. The local-deployment category is the priority, because it is the one the draft places within export management [2]. For each locally deployed asset, teams should ask the supplier in writing whether it has registered the export under Announcement No. 48 and whether it expects to need a license once the catalogue is final.

Legal and engineering teams should jointly review technology flows out of China-based subsidiaries, joint ventures, and R&D centers since October 16. The goal is to identify transfers that may already require registration, including code repositories, model checkpoints, and agent frameworks shared with overseas affiliates [2][4]. Organizations with a material interest in the final scope should prepare comments before the November 15, 2026 deadline, through the email, fax, or postal channels published in the announcement [1][4].

Short-Term Mitigations

Over the next one to two quarters, organizations should treat restricted-category Chinese models as regulated dependencies with documented fallbacks. Vendor contracts for locally deployed models should allocate responsibility for Chinese export registration and licensing, specify notice obligations if a license is denied, conditioned, or revoked, and address whether updates and new checkpoints are covered by the same authorization. Because the “global leading” test depends on rankings at the time of export [1], teams should not assume that a model version cleared today will remain uncontrolled for later updates.

Security teams that rely on AI-assisted vulnerability discovery or deepfake detection tools developed in China should map those tools against the restricted thresholds and identify alternatives. A licensing interruption to a detection capability is a security-control gap, not only a procurement issue. Data governance teams should also extend Data Security Law classification work to cover training and fine-tuning datasets held in China, so that “important data” and “core data” exposure is known before models trained on them are shared abroad [1].

Strategic Considerations

Announcement No. 48, if finalized substantially as drafted, would mean that frontier AI is treated as controlled technology by both the United States and China, with each regime drawing its lines differently. Recent U.S. measures have emphasized compute and, in the Fable 5 case, access to a deployed model, although the since-rescinded 2025 AI Diffusion rule also reached model weights [3]. The Chinese draft centers on custody of weights, know-how, and agent architectures. Enterprise AI governance programs should model export-control disruption from either jurisdiction as a standing risk scenario and design architectures that can swap models without rebuilding agent workflows.

Organizations should also recognize that the draft treats agents as a distinct regulatory object. Defining controls by planning depth, concurrency, and tool count means that internal agent platforms, and not only foundation models, may be subject to cross-border technology rules. Agent inventories should record these characteristics alongside traditional security attributes. Finally, because the final catalogue may narrow, broaden, or shift after consultation [3], and because ChinaTalk notes the comment window closes shortly before an expected leaders’ meeting at APEC [3], a timing that could bear on the final scope, this analysis should be revisited once MOFCOM publishes the final text.

CSA Resource Alignment

CSA’s most directly relevant prior work is Frontier AI Export Controls: Enterprise Governance After Fable 5 [8]. That note argues for treating frontier model access as a contingent operational dependency that belongs in vendor management and business continuity planning. Announcement No. 48 extends that argument to a second jurisdiction and to a different control point. The U.S. action examined in that note interrupted service access, while the Chinese draft leaves service access untouched and instead governs weight custody and local deployment. Enterprises that built continuity plans around the U.S. scenario should check whether those plans also cover a supplier-side license failure for self-hosted models.

AI Model Export Controls: The Fable 5 Precedent [9] documented how a single regulatory directive can remove a widely deployed model with little notice. Its recommendation for multi-model fallback strategies applies directly to organizations that depend on Chinese frontier or open-weight models, particularly given the dynamic “global leading” threshold described above. Sovereign AI Access Controls and Enterprise Concentration Risk [10] provides the broader framing. It treats national control over AI capability as a source of concentration risk, and the Chinese draft is a concrete instance of that risk materializing on the supply side.

For control implementation, the AI Controls Matrix (AICM) v1.1 [11] provides the relevant control objectives in its supply chain management, transparency and accountability, and governance, risk and compliance domains, including supplier inventory, third-party assessment, and regulatory change management. For agent-specific exposure, MAESTRO [12] offers a layered threat model that can help teams document the agent capabilities, such as tool integration and multi-agent coordination, that now carry export-control significance.

References

[1] Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology of the PRC. “Announcement No. 48 of 2026 on Public Consultation on Revising the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export and Interim Registration of Related Technology Exports (商务部 科技部公告2026年第48号), with Annex 1 (Draft Scope of AI, Biomedicine, and Photovoltaic Technologies).” MOFCOM, October 16, 2026.

[3] Ennis, Q., Zhang, I., Ottinger, L., and Zakaria, A. “MOFCOM’s New Rules and the Future of Chinese AI.” ChinaTalk, October 21, 2026.

[5] Sun, R. “China’s AI Export Control Announcement Raises More Questions Than It Answers.” Ctrl+AI+Reg, October 19, 2026.

The beginning of BSD Unix

When Ken Thompson returned to Bell Labs in 1976, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley began exploring the Unix kernel themselves.

Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel.

Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler.

Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape.

In early 1977, Bill Joy put together the Berkeley Software Distribution, or BSD, bundling the Pascal system with ex, a line editor developed from em. Early BSD was not a standalone operating system: it was a collection of software to install on an existing Unix system. About thirty copies were sent out over the following year.[1]

At the time, an AT&T Unix source license was needed to get BSD. Berkeley charged only for the tape and distribution.[2]

If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage.

Berkeley already had a tradition of sharing research software. BSD carried it on. Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, hippie culture, and antiwar activism are also said to have influenced Joy's decision to charge so little.[2]

Universities and research institutions could obtain Unix, including its source code, for a modest licensing fee. This also helped the system spread.[2][6]

We have Unix, but the antitrust agreement bars us from the computer business... We can't sell it as a product, either.

The second distribution: 2BSD

After the first BSD distribution, Joy improved the Pascal system based on user feedback. He bundled it with vi (ex's visual mode), the C shell, and other tools to form the Second Berkeley Software Distribution, or 2BSD. Nearly seventy-five tapes were shipped over the following year.[1][5]

Joy did more than fix bugs. He handled every distribution request, copied BSD onto tapes, and mailed them out himself.

Oh, you need a copy of BSD?

Another university wants a copy.

Tune the kernel. Fix the bugs.

A VAX arrives at Berkeley, 1978

Professor Fateman's group is getting a VAX. It's 32-bit, with a whole megabyte of memory.

Really? We should put Unix on it.

They've already got VAX Unix from Bell Labs. It's called 32/V.

My adviser asked me to add virtual memory to VAX Unix. Could you look over the code?

Babaoglu was a Berkeley graduate student working with Professor Domenico Ferrari. Joy helped him integrate the virtual-memory code into 32/V and debug it.[1][4]

At the time, 32/V did not use the VAX hardware's virtual-memory capabilities. A program's address space was limited by physical memory, but Professor Richard Fateman's work on the computer algebra system Macsyma needed more. Virtual memory uses disk storage to give programs an address space larger than physical memory.[1]

Macsyma, developed at MIT beginning in the late 1960s, worked with symbolic expressions. It could factor expressions, compute derivatives, and perform integration.

Debugging continued through the holidays at the end of 1978.

Not going away for the holidays?

Might as well debug this while fewer people are using the VAX.

By January 1979, most of the bugs had been fixed.[1]

Let's try Unix with virtual memory.

Finally. It runs without crashing.

Joy ported ex, vi, the C shell, and other 2BSD tools to the VAX, while Peter Kessler and Marshall Kirk McKusick ported the Pascal system. These programs were bundled with the standard 32/V utilities and the virtual-memory kernel that Babaoglu and Joy had integrated and debugged. The result was 3BSD, which began shipping in December 1979.[1]

At last, we can send these out.

Since 1969, ARPANET had linked research institutions funded by DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.[3] But these institutions used different computers and operating systems, so they often couldn't share software. Porting the existing software to new machines was also costly. DARPA became interested in Unix's portability, and took notice of Berkeley's successful distribution of 3BSD to research institutions.[1]

BSD runs pretty well on this VAX.

References

  1. Marshall Kirk McKusick, Twenty Years of Berkeley Unix, in Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution, 1999. Korean edition, Hanbit Media, 2013.
  2. Andrew Leonard, BSD Unix: Power to the people, from the code, Salon, 2000.
  3. SRI International, ARPANET. Its origins and the first transmission in 1969.
  4. Ozalp Babaoglu, Biographical note. His Unix virtual-memory research as a Berkeley graduate student.
  5. The Unix Heritage Society (TUHS), Original 2BSD distribution archive. The installation document install.ms and source code in 2bsd.tar.gz.
  6. Warren Toomey, The Strange Birth and Long Life of Unix, IEEE Spectrum, 2011.

Est. October 2026 · Apache-2.0

OccupySaaS is a protest movement written in code. Laid-off engineers, armed with AI and public documentation, are building clean-room, open-source, drop-in replacements for the platforms that rent our own industry back to us — one seat at a time.

We are the
1,000,000

The grievances

The software built
by the 99% belongs
to the 99%.

In 2011, Occupy Wall Street asked who the economy was really working for. In 2026 we're asking the same question about the cloud. The tools every company runs on are now toll booths — and the people who built them were shown the door.

Per-seat pricing is a tax on growth

Every hire, every intern, every contractor — another line item. Infrastructure shouldn't charge rent by the head.

Lock-in is not a feature

Proprietary APIs, export walls and surprise price hikes keep customers captive. Compatible open alternatives set them free.

They cut us. We commit.

A million engineers were let go while the platforms kept growing. We still know how to ship. Now we ship it in the open.

The method

Clean room.
AI rebuild.
Drop-in.

We don't leak, decompile or copy anyone's code. Every project is rebuilt from public documentation and open standards, with AI doing the heavy lifting on the build side of a strict firewall — then proven compatible against the vendors' own public SDKs.

  1. Read the public record

    Public API references, open standards (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, REST) and published SDK behaviour become a written specification. Nothing confidential, nothing leaked, nothing from former employers.

  2. Raise the firewall

    Spec writers and builders stay separated. Each repo carries a CLEAN_ROOM.md policy, and provenance is recorded for every fixture and reference.

  3. Rebuild with AI

    AI agents implement from the spec alone — contracts first (openapi.yaml), then code, then tests — under human review at every merge.

  4. Prove compatibility

    A compatibility laboratory runs the vendors' own public client SDKs against our server. If your existing code doesn't work unchanged, it isn't done.

  5. Release it to everyone

    Apache-2.0. Self-hostable. Pluggable storage. No telemetry you didn't ask for, and no seat counter.

Allowed in →

  • Public API docs
  • Open standards & RFCs
  • Public SDK behaviour
  • Black-box test results

Clean room

× Never allowed

  • Leaked or proprietary source
  • Decompiled binaries
  • Former-employer confidential info
  • Copied UI assets or trademarks

First releases

Two towers
occupied.

Identity and CRM: the two subscriptions almost every company pays for and almost nobody loves. Both are early, both are public, and both welcome contributors today.

Early · in the open Go

ZeroAuthy

A self-hostable identity server that speaks the Auth0 Authentication API. Point an existing Auth0 SDK at a ZeroAuthy tenant domain and it works with no code changes.

  • OIDC discovery, JWKS & multi-tenant domains
  • Hosted login, authorization code + PKCE
  • client_credentials, rotating refresh tokens, revoke & logout
  • Verified with auth0-spa-js, auth0-react & nextjs-auth0
# build & run
$ go build -o bin/zeroauthy ./cmd/zeroauthy
$ ./bin/zeroauthy serve --config config.yaml
$ curl https://localhost:8443/.well-known/openid-configuration

SQLitePostgreSQLMySQLgRPC pluginsApache-2.0

Early · in the open Go · Vue · TypeScript

SalesCompel

A free, open-source Salesforce replacement with a tenant-isolated Go/PostgreSQL core, a Vue record editor, and a compatibility laboratory that checks behaviour against Salesforce's public API contract.

  • Persistent Account & Contact CRUD
  • Object describe and limited queries
  • External-ID upsert & bearer authentication
  • OpenAPI 3.2 REST contract & offline test lab
# run the compatibility laboratory
$ npm ci --prefix compat/clients/node --ignore-scripts
$ npm --prefix compat/clients/node run check

The occupation map

Who's next?

Every category on this board is a monthly invoice somewhere. The movement picks the next target in public — bring a spec, a use case, or a grudge.

● Occupied

Identity & Auth

ZeroAuthy — Auth0-compatible login, tokens and tenants.

● Occupied

CRM

SalesCompel — Salesforce-compatible records and REST API.

○ Proposed

Docs & Wikis

Team knowledge bases that don't lock your writing behind a seat licence.

○ Proposed

Issue Tracking

Tickets, sprints and boards with a compatible API for existing integrations.

○ Proposed

Feature Flags

SDK-compatible flag evaluation you can run next to your own services.

○ Proposed

Observability

Logs, metrics and traces without per-gigabyte ransom notes.

○ Proposed

Customer Support

Help desk, inbox and knowledge base, priced at zero agents.

+ Your pick

Propose a target

Open an issue and make the case.

Proposed categories are open for discussion, not commitments. Names of existing products are used only to describe compatibility.

Lineage

From Zuccotti Park
to git push.

Occupy Wall Street began on 17 September 2011 in Zuccotti Park, New York City, with a simple frame: the 1% and the 99%. It had no leaders, made decisions in open assemblies, and spread to hundreds of cities.

OccupySaaS borrows that spirit and swaps tents for terminals. No marches, no property damage — just working software, published under an open licence, that anyone can run.

“We are the 99%.”

  1. 17 Sep 2011 Occupy Wall Street begins

    Protesters set up camp in Zuccotti Park in Manhattan's Financial District.

  2. Oct 2011 The movement spreads

    Occupy camps and general assemblies appear in cities around the world.

  3. 15 Nov 2011 Zuccotti Park is cleared

    The camp ends; the language of the 1% and the 99% doesn't.

  4. 2022 – 2025 The great tech layoffs

    Wave after wave of cuts across the industry while subscription prices keep climbing.

  5. 14 Oct 2026 ZeroAuthy goes public

    The first clean-room rebuild opens its repo under Apache-2.0.

  6. 15 Oct 2026 SalesCompel joins the occupation

    The second tower. More to come — decided in the open.

Join

Occupy everything.

You don't need permission, a badge or a manager. You need a laptop and an afternoon.

Write code

Pick an open issue, follow the clean-room policy, open a pull request.

Self-host it

Run a release against your real SDKs and tell us exactly where it breaks.

Write specs

Turn public docs into precise, testable specifications for the builders.

Make noise

Star the repos, share the site, and tell your CFO what you're paying per seat.

Is this legal?

Clean-room reimplementation is a long-established way to build compatible software: you work only from public information and independently write your own code. Interoperating with an API is not the same as copying a product. Each project publishes its clean-room policy and source provenance so anyone can check the work. This page isn't legal advice; if you're adopting a project for a business, talk to your own counsel.

Are you affiliated with Auth0, Okta or Salesforce?

No. OccupySaaS and its projects are independent and not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor named on this site. Product names are used only to describe compatibility.

Can former employees of those companies contribute?

Yes, but never with confidential knowledge from a former employer. Contributors work only from public material, and anyone with relevant inside knowledge should stay on the public-spec side of the firewall or sit that project out. When in doubt, read the project's CLEAN_ROOM.md and ask first.

Why use AI to build it?

Because the giants had thousands of engineers and we have a movement. AI agents let a small group turn a precise spec into working code quickly. Humans write the specs, review every change, and own the result, and compatibility tests against real SDKs decide what counts as done.

Why Go?

Portability. A Go project compiles to a single self-contained binary, so self-hosting means dropping one file onto a server or into a Docker or Podman image — no installer, no runtime to set up, no tree of shared libraries to keep in sync. The same toolchain cross-compiles for Linux, macOS, Windows, x86 and ARM, and the result fits in a minimal container image. If you're leaving a SaaS vendor, the replacement should be this easy to carry.

Why not Rust?

Nothing is wrong with Rust, and we're not against it. Go was picked for the first projects because it makes the one-file, container-friendly drop-in the default with very little build setup. Rust can get there too; Go just gets there more simply for the kind of servers we're building.

Rust recreations of these projects are welcome — they just haven't been made yet. The specs, API contracts and compatibility tests are language-neutral, so a Rust port can be checked against the same SDKs. If you want to start one, open an issue and say which project.

Is it production-ready?

Not yet. Both first projects are early and say so plainly in their READMEs, along with exactly which features work today. Try them, break them, and file issues.

What does it cost?

Nothing. Every project is released under the Apache License 2.0. Run it, fork it, sell services around it. The only thing we ask is that you contribute back what you can.
